newsitem.title: USA: Arrest warrants sought for Texas separatists.
newsitem.headline: Arrest warrants sought for Texas separatists.

text.p: Texas police Monday sought arrest warrants for members of an armed separatist group holed up in a mountain compound and said special tactics teams were being flown to the scene.

Texas Department of Public Safety spokesman Mike Cox would not say if the police planned to move in to arrest the members of the group, the Republic of Texas, but said in a press conference: "Hopefully we won't have to be here too long."

The threat of a violent end to the standoff sent residents living near the compound in the remote Davis Mountains of west Texas scurrying from their homes. Cox said they would not be allowed back in until the situation was resolved.

Authorities also imposed a ban on flights below 5,000 feet within a five-mile radius of the area, Cox said. Several SWAT teams would arrive Monday night from Austin, Texas, when the arrest warrants charging members of the Republic of Texas with kidnapping, burglary and aggravated assault were expected to be issued by a local judge, he added.
The standoff began Sunday after Republic members took two hostages in retaliation for the arrest of their security chief Bob Scheidt.
Cox said the hostages, middle-age couple Joe and Margaret Rowe, were seized in a hail of bullets by three Republic members who stormed their home near the compound in full battle gear.
Joe Rowe was injured in the attack, either by a bullet or flying glass, and was beaten with gunbutts, Cox said.
Police surrounded the area and after 12 hours of negotiations, the Rowes were released in exchange for the return of Scheidt to the group's compound. Rowe was said to be in fair condition.

Scheidt was arrested when Jeff Davis County Sheriff Steve Bailey found an AK-47 and other illegal arms in Scheidt's car. Bailey stopped Scheidt while responding to calls that residents of the area had seen men in camouflage uniforms trespassing on their property, Cox said.

Police did not know why the Republic of Texas members were allegedly moving about in camouflage uniforms, Cox said, but the group has been stirring up trouble for at least two years with demands that Texas secede from the United States.

Republic leaders claim Texas' 1845 annexation into the United States was unconstitutional and demand that the Lone Star state be recognised as a sovereign nation with themselves as its provisional leaders. Texas was an independent nation for nine years after it broke away from Mexico in 1836.
The Republic group set up its own court system and militia units, and has since filed thousands of liens against government agencies and private property owners.

State officials said the liens are bogus and are aimed at clogging up the state's courts. They also accuse the group of using millions of dollars of fraudulent but official looking checks made out in the name of the Republic of Texas.

Richard McLaren, self-styled leader of the Republic, said the group's actions are legitimate because its courts last year issued a $93 trillion lien against the U.S. government, the United Nations and the Roman Catholic Church for allegedly plundering Texas' wealth over 150 years.

McLaren was charged with contempt of court last December for failing to appear in a federal court in nearby Pecos on charges related to the liens. Since then, he and a number of followers have holed up inside their compound, which is about 200 miles southeast of El Paso, Texas, sending out their separatist message by fax and the Internet.

Police, mindful of the disastrous conclusion to similar standoffs at Ruby Ridge, Idaho and the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas, did not arrest McLaren because of fears sparking a violent clash.
